title: Norm denominators: all x, y, z sums of two squares — fails at 16 primes below 4000
connection: Requiring every denominator to be a norm from Z[i] (sum of two squares) fails at p = 41, 137, 233, 241, 601, 769, … (16 of 269). This is the 'Gaussian-norm' constrained world.
why: A constrained world with visible failures is a laboratory: if its failures have a local/reciprocity explanation it is a cousin of T1; if not, it is a lottery world at a lower expected count.
first_step: Up to 2·10^4: 40 failures among 1125 primes (data/z52b/analogues_constraints_20000.txt). Test whether failures are density-zero, and check whether a local obstruction (e.g. mod 8 or mod 3) explains them.
refs: scripts/z52b_analogues_constraints.py (p ≡ 1 mod 4, p < 4000, all solutions enumerated)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: z is a common multiple of x and y: fails only at p = 2521 below 2·10^4
connection: Solutions with x | z and y | z exist for every p ≡ 1 mod 4 below 4000 except 2521. This sub-world is almost as rich as ES.
why: A near-complete subfamily with a single small exception is an excellent candidate for a structural theorem 'ES with lcm = max denominator for p > p₀' and indicates a rich parametrisation.
first_step: Still only 2521 below 2·10^4 (data/z52b/analogues_constraints_20000.txt). Parametrize lcm-solutions (z = lcm) explicitly and run to 10^6 to see if exceptions stay sparse; inspect 2521 = 2521 (prime) for special structure.
refs: scripts/z52b_analogues_constraints.py (p ≡ 1 mod 4, p < 4000, all solutions enumerated)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Denominators ≡ 1 (mod 3) is impossible when 3 ∤ n: a 3-adic obstruction
connection: If x, y, z ≡ 1 mod 3 then 1/x + 1/y + 1/z ≡ 3 ≡ 0 in Z_(3), while 4/n is a 3-adic unit when 3 ∤ n. More generally, with k terms and denominators ≡ 1 mod ℓ, one needs 4/n ≡ k (mod ℓ).
why: Shows that 'number of terms ≡ 0 mod ℓ' interacts with congruence-restricted denominators; a family of worlds where obstructions depend on k mod ℓ.
first_step: Tabulate for ℓ ∈ {3,5,7}, H = subgroup of (Z/ℓ)^*, the classes of n for which ES_H is locally obstructed.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Pairwise coprime denominators: impossible for n ≥ 2
connection: If gcd(x,y) = gcd(y,z) = gcd(x,z) = 1, the fraction (xy+yz+zx)/xyz is already reduced, so xyz = n·t and xy + yz + zx = 4t with t = 1, impossible for positive integers. All solutions need shared factors among denominators.
why: Every solution has a 'gcd skeleton'; the repo's Type I/II parametrisation is exactly the description of that skeleton. A constrained world with exactly one coprime pair is a natural middle case.
first_step: Count, for p < 4000, solutions with exactly one coprime pair vs none (the computation shows 'all pairs share a factor' never fails).
refs: scripts/z52b_analogues_constraints.py (p ≡ 1 mod 4, p < 4000, all solutions enumerated)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Signed ES with a size-controlled negative term: 4/n = 1/x + 1/y − 1/z with z ≥ n^{1+δ}
connection: Signed ES is trivial (4/(4k+1) = 1/k − 1/(k(4k+1))). Requiring the negative term to be tiny (z large) interpolates between trivial and ES-like. Find the threshold δ at which signed ES stops being covered by identities.
why: A threshold statement would be a new integer theorem halfway to ES, and the identity families near threshold are candidates to perturb into positive solutions.
first_step: For p ≤ 10^4, compute the maximal z over signed solutions with one negative term; check whether z ≥ p³ is always achievable (via identities).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Semiprime denominators: 4/p as a sum of three reciprocals of semiprimes
connection: Recent work shows every natural number is a sum of distinct semiprime unit fractions (Shisheng Li). The 3-term version for 4/p is a constrained ES with a natural density of allowed denominators ~ log log x / log x.
why: Probes how ES's solution count scales when denominators are thinned to a density-zero but not too sparse set.
first_step: Brute force for p ≤ 10^4; record failure density; compare with lottery prediction.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES restricted to 'Type I only' or 'Type II only': two sub-worlds with known almost-all behaviour
connection: Elsholtz–Tao distinguish Type I (p divides one denominator) and Type II (p divides two). Each sub-world is a constrained ES; which primes need Type II? (Computation: 'y, z both divisible by p' never fails below 4000; 'only z divisible by p' never fails either.)
why: Since both sub-worlds appear complete numerically, each is a strengthening of ES and may be easier to attack structurally (one family of divisor conditions).
first_step: Extend to 10^6: does 'Type II only' (p | y, p | z) ever fail? (Repo has censuses—check I3/Type II data first.)
refs: scripts/z52b_analogues_constraints.py (p ≡ 1 mod 4, p < 4000, all solutions enumerated)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Size-capped ES: max denominator ≤ p²/8 fails at 45 primes below 2·10^4 (incl. 5, 13, 17, 29)
connection: The cap z ≤ p²/8 removes the largest solutions (Type II with z ≍ p²); 45 primes then fail. The failure set shows which primes depend on the 'extreme' solutions.
why: Size-capped worlds quantify how much ES relies on huge denominators; the threshold cap c(p) = min over solutions of z/p² is a new invariant.
first_step: Compute c(p) = min_solutions max(x,y,z)/p² for p < 2·10^4; check whether c(p) → 0 or stays bounded below for infinitely many p.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Type II with x not divisible by p never fails below 2·10^4
connection: Solutions with p | y, p | z, p ∤ x exist for every p ≡ 1 mod 4 below 2·10^4. This is the 'pure Type II' strengthening (Elsholtz–Tao notation).
why: A sub-world that is complete in range and has the cleanest divisor parametrization (divisors of a p-tied integer in one class) is the natural proof target.
first_step: Compare with the repo's existing Type II censuses (Z52_BANKED / I3 censuses) to avoid duplication; then count pure-Type-II solutions vs log²p.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Function-field random-matrix model applied over Z: Katz–Sarnak symmetry type of ES counts?
connection: If the FF fixed-P ES count is a trace of a Frobenius on some cohomology (sum over Type II data), its fluctuations follow a symmetry type (U, Sp, O). Over Z the same symmetry type would predict lower-tail probabilities.
why: A symmetry type predicts how often the count is near zero, which is the ES question at a single p.
first_step: Compute FF fixed-P counts for q = 3, deg P = 8, normalize, and compare histogram with Sato–Tate/semicircle/other Katz–Sarnak laws.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES in 'Z with a different order': positive cone = {n : n ≡ 1 mod 4 or …} is not multiplicatively closed — design check
connection: Orders on Z other than the usual one don't exist (Z has a unique ordering as an ordered ring). So 'other positivity on Z' must be a semigroup restriction (constraint worlds), not a new order.
why: Closes a tempting but empty direction; constraint worlds (batch C) cover the meaningful variants.
first_step: None (closed).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Categorified ES over N[T]: identities with non-negative coefficient polynomials, evaluated at T = 1
connection: If 4/P(T) = Σ 1/X_i(T) with X_i ∈ N[T] and P(1) = n, evaluation at T = 1 gives ES for n and at T = 2, 3, … ES for P(2), P(3), …. So N[T]-solutions are 'categorified' solutions propagating to an infinite family.
why: For a given n, choosing P with P(1) = n freely might make the N[T]-problem easier than ES (more freedom in P), yet it implies ES at n. Conversely Mordell–Schinzel forbids it when P(T) hits square classes at many T.
first_step: For n = 5, 13, 17, search P ∈ N[T] of degree ≤ 2 with P(1) = n and an N[T]-identity of low degree; check what values P(T) take mod 840.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES over Z_(p) (all primes except p inverted, ordering inherited from Q): trivial
connection: Z_(p) ⊂ Q inherits the usual order. Since 4 is invertible in Z_(p) for odd p, 4/p = 1/(p/2) + 1/p + 1/p with positive denominators p/2, p, p ∈ Z_(p). So inverting everything but p trivializes ES — the complementary extreme to Z[1/p].
why: Boundary marker for the localization family; the interesting worlds are finite S (Z[1/ℓ]) where structure remains.
first_step: None (closed).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Function-field Gaussian twin: F_q[T][√−T] or F_q[T, i] with a 'sector' sign
connection: The Gaussian cone twin has an FF analogue: an imaginary quadratic function field with a sign on both 'real and imaginary' parts (e.g. leading coefficients). Combining the two analogue directions gives a doubly-twisted world where computation is easy.
why: If the FF-Gaussian twin is proved (by FF methods) while the Z-Gaussian twin is open, the transfer gap is the same as for ES — confirming the gap is archimedean, not about i.
first_step: Define the sign function on F_q[T][√D] for D of odd degree (imaginary quadratic FF) and run the e-slice search.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES_q(T) has no finite linear covering for q = 3^r, r ≥ 2 (FF_ODD_ABSENCE Cor 2.3) — a proved FF 'Mordell'
connection: The FF analogue of Mordell's no-covering result is PROVED for q = 9, 27, … (computer-assisted); in contrast F_4 and F_2 have finite coverings. This maps exactly which q behave like Z with respect to coverings.
why: Characterizing q with/without finite coverings (char 2 yes, 3^r no) gives a criterion whose Z-analogue is Mordell; the char-2 exception is the cancellation mechanism.
first_step: Tabulate known covering status for q ∈ {2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9}; guess the criterion (char 2 ⇔ covering?).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Fixed q = 3 resembles Z (EXSET_FUNCTION_FIELD #10): use F_3[T] as the Z simulator
connection: At q = 3, non-square failures vanish at odd n ≤ 15 and are few at even n, with no irreducible failure beyond n = 8 — Z-like behaviour. F_3[T] is the best 'simulator' of Z among FF worlds.
why: Any claimed integer mechanism can be stress-tested in F_3[T] with exact enumeration to large degree, where the analogous statement is checkable.
first_step: Adopt a rule: every proposed ES mechanism gets an F_3[T] translation and a degree ≤ 15 test before Z work.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Signed ES with exactly one negative term and all |denominators| ≤ C·n²: does it always hold?
connection: Signed ES (one minus sign) is trivially solvable with denominators ≍ n² (4/(4k+1) = 1/k − 1/(k(4k+1)), split one more). Bounding all three denominators by C·n² keeps it easy; bounding by n^{3/2} may make it a lottery.
why: A signed analogue with a size cap is a tunable world: its threshold exponent vs the positive ES threshold (> 3/2 from data) compares sign freedom with size freedom.
first_step: For n ≤ 10^4 compute the minimal max-denominator over signed (one negative) 3-term representations of 4/n; compare growth with the positive case.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Signed ES with two negative terms: 4/n = 1/x − 1/y − 1/z — trivial, and what that shows
connection: 1/x − 1/y − 1/z = 4/n with x < n/4: choose x = ⌊n/4⌋ (or nearby) and represent the positive difference by 1/y + 1/z — becomes a 2-term positive problem for the difference, often solvable but not always.
why: Sign patterns (+,+,+), (+,+,−), (+,−,−) form a ladder: (+,+,−) trivial, (+,−,−) reduces to 2-term problems, (+,+,+) is ES. The (+,−,−) case is a natural intermediate.
first_step: For n ≤ 10^4 test (+,−,−) solvability with a bounded first term; list failures.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Signed ES as the 'char-2 shadow': cancellation of equal-size terms ↔ difference of nearly equal unit fractions
connection: In F_2[T], 1/X + 1/(X + δ) has a cancelled leading term; over Z, 1/x − 1/(x + δ) = δ/(x(x+δ)) is small. Signed integer identities in which the negative term is the partner of a positive term mimic F₂ identities.
why: Lifting F₂-proofs to Z would produce signed identities; a 'positivity repair' lemma (replace 1/a − 1/b by positive terms when structure allows) would complete the transfer.
first_step: Take the F₂[T] covering identities (FUNCTIONFIELD_ES §6), substitute T ↦ 2 or T ↦ integer with signs, and see which become signed integer identities for 4/n.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Matrix ES with nilpotent perturbations: X = xI + N (unipotent-type) over Z
connection: For X = xI + N with N nilpotent (N² = 0), X⁻¹ = (1/x)I − N/x². Matrix ES with such X reduces to ES plus the linear condition Σ N_i/x_i² = 0 — the dual-number world in matrix form.
why: Connects the dual-number item to matrices: solvable whenever the tangent condition is, so it's a 'first-order' matrix world.
first_step: Record equivalence; test the tangent condition on ES solutions for small p (shared with dual-number item).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Matrix ES in M_2(Z) with X symmetric positive-definite and det X = x: projective version
connection: For PD integral X with det X = x, (X⁻¹)_{11} = X_{22}/x. Summing (1,1) entries: 4/n = Σ X_i,22/x_i — numerators X_i,22 ≥ 1, so the (1,1)-projection gives a 'numerator-weighted ES'. Matrix ES ⇒ weighted ES with weights X_{22}.
why: Weighted ES with weights ≥ 1 is easier (weights 2 trivialize), so matrix ES is likely easy; this pins how the matrix world relaxes ES.
first_step: Check whether k = 2 matrix ES is trivially solvable via weighted identities (e.g. one matrix contributing weight 2).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Monic F_q[T] with A = 4 (constant) in char 3: trivially true since 4 = 1
connection: In char 3, 4 = 1, so ES_q(4, P) = ES_q(1, P) is trivial (1/P = 1/(P+1) + 1/(P(P+1)) split once more). Constant numerators reduce mod p; only polynomial numerators are faithful.
why: Boundary marker: shows why the faithful FF analogue uses deg A ≥ 1.
first_step: Record.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Sign-twisted FF world: monic denominators but numerator A with leading coefficient c ≠ 1
connection: With A of leading coefficient c, Lemma 1.1 forces lc relations; choosing c a non-square (q odd) twists the 'colour' at ∞ — an FF analogue of changing the numerator's sign class (4 vs −4 or 4 vs 4·non-square).
why: Over Z the analogous twist is numerator −4 (signed) or 4·(−1) — trivial; in FF the twist by non-square c is non-trivial and may model T1's sign layer.
first_step: Run ES_q(cT, P) for q = 3, c = −1 (non-square), deg P ≤ 10; compare with c = 1.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Feature: function-field / large-q degeneration
connection: Dividing-line feature 'function-field / large-q degeneration'. ES HAS proved variants over F_q[T]. To supply it one could: identify which F_q[T] proof step (RH for curves, large-q equidistribution) has an integer analogue in a 'large auxiliary parameter' regime
why: Twin primes / Artin are proved over F_q[T] via RH for curves where ℤ needs GRH-plus.
first_step: From FUNCTIONFIELD_ES*.md, extract the exact F_q[T] theorem and its 'q → ∞' mechanism.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Between: ES over rings of integers O_K with total positivity
connection: Define ES_K: 4/ν = 1/ξ + 1/η + 1/ζ with totally positive ξ, η, ζ ∈ O_K. Does it fail for some K (e.g. Q(√2), Q(√5))?
why: If ES_K fails for a real quadratic K, the failing mechanism (units? positivity at two places?) is a candidate obstruction for ES itself; if it holds via the same covering identities, it's a calibration.
first_step: Search ES_K for K = Q(√2), Q(√5) for small totally positive primes ν with a bounded-height search.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Archimedean variant: 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z with x, y, z ∈ ℤ allowing one negative denominator
connection: With one negative denominator the problem changes count regime (infinitely many solutions?) and becomes identity-solvable; the dividing line between 'all positive' and 'one negative' measures the positivity cost.
why: Isolates positivity as the obstacle (feature item 'positivity as the whole content').
first_step: Find explicit identities for 4/p = 1/x + 1/y − 1/z valid for all p; check known literature (it is classical that signed versions are easy).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: '3-divisible ES': 12/p fails at 22 primes ≤ 10⁵, last 12 241
why: Contains the Type-A failures 193 and 2521 and the R-zero 577: the '3-divisible' sub-problem is hard on the same primes — a sub-ES whose failure set is a fingerprint of global hardness.
first_step: Extend 12/p to 10⁷ (fast: x ∈ (p/12, p/4]) to test finiteness; check whether 66529, 409, 5569 eventually appear (they do not ≤ 10⁵ except as listed).
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: '5-divisible ES': 20/p fails at 63 primes ≤ 10⁵, last 90001
connection: No ES solution with 5 | x, y, z at 63 primes ≤ 10⁵, including 1201, 2521, 4201, 4801, 8761, 21841, 24481 (ES-hard) — the last at 90001 = 9·10⁴+1.
why: The 5-divisible failure set mirrors primes ≡ 1 (mod 5^a·…) — a local obstruction at 5 that compounds global hardness.
first_step: Tabulate p mod 25 and mod 125 for 20/p failures vs random primes.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Divisibility-strengthened ES_k ladder (k | x,y,z): last failures 241, 12241, 83449, 90001, ≥97777, 92401, …
why: PW prove n_m ≥ exp(m^{1/3+o(1)}), so ES_k fails infinitely far out as k grows but each ES_k plausibly has finitely many failures — a quantitative family 'between' ES and false statements, useful to calibrate any method's strength (a method proving ES_k for k=3 would be stronger than ES).
first_step: Pick the smallest k (k=2, 'even ES') and try to push the census to 10¹⁰ with a dedicated sieve; check whether the 8/n exceptions really stop at 241.
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Joint failure: no prime ≤ 10⁵ fails both 8/p and 12/p beyond {2,3}
connection: fail(8) ∩ fail(12) = {2,3}; fail(8) ∩ fail(16) = fail(8) by monotonicity; overlaps of non-nested failure sets are small.
why: Different divisibility strengthenings fail on disjoint primes; a covering-by-subfamilies proof (each prime gets an even OR 3-divisible solution) is numerically plausible: 'ES_2 ∪ ES_3 covers all p > 3'.
first_step: Verify 'every prime p > 3 has an ES solution with all-even or all-3-divisible denominators' to 10⁷, and find the minimal such union family.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: A union conjecture: ES_2 ∪ ES_3 (even or 3-divisible solutions) for all primes p > 3
connection: Since fail(8) ∩ fail(12) ∩ primes = {2,3} ≤ 10⁵, conjecture: every prime p > 3 has an ES solution with 2 | x,y,z or 3 | x,y,z.
why: Each subfamily has a cleaner local structure (2-adic resp. 3-adic) than ES; a proof could exploit that the obstructions live at different primes (analogous to López's Type A ∪ Type B conjecture).
first_step: Extend the joint census; search for the natural certificate lines in each subfamily and check whether their failure sets are disjoint.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Last 16/p failure 83449 and last 12/p failure 12241: next-term prediction
connection: If ES_k failure sets are finite, the largest elements grow quickly with k; PW-type heuristics would predict last(ES_k) ≈ exp(c k^{1/3}) or similar.
why: A cheap predictive check of the probabilistic model behind PW on the ES-relevant numerators 4k.
first_step: Fit log last(4k) for k = 2..5 and compare with PW's density model; extend 16/p and 20/p to 10⁷ to see if new failures appear.
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Tail law of Cmin vs independent divisor events
connection: If the slice failures F_C = {4Cp+1 has no divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4C)} were independent, P(Cmin > c) ≈ ∏_{C≤c} P(F_C), where each P(F_C) decays slowly with p (a single-shift failure law, cf. EXSET_SHIFT_DIVISORS Thm 2.2); compare with data. Also compute the full correlation matrix of the events E_C = ¬F_C for C ≤ 20–32 (φ-coefficients; E_C and E_{2C} share structure).
why: Measures dependence between (★) slices C — exactly the 'joint budget' question (JOINT_BUDGET.md) in a cheap observable.
first_step: Compute empirical P(E_C) and P(E_C ∩ E_C′) at p ≤ 3·10⁶ for C, C′ ≤ 20; report the correlation matrix.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Union of restricted families: smallest set of shapes covering all primes
connection: Shapes with tiny failure sets ≤ 10⁵: lcm-closed {2521}; all-squarefree {71, 191, 21169}; none-div-by-3 {3, 241}; some-denominator-div-by-4 {2, 17, 241}. lcm-closed ∪ none-div-by-3 covers every prime ≤ 10⁵ (lcm-closed certifies 3). Not all pairs are disjoint: none-div-by-3 and 4-divides-some both fail at 241.
why: Each shape has its own local structure; a proof of 'every p has an lcm-closed or 3-free solution' might be easier than ES if the two obstructions are incompatible (2521 vs 241 are different local profiles).
first_step: Find the local reason for each single exception and test whether any prime can fail two shapes simultaneously (search to 10⁷).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Function-field analogue of 2521: polynomials ≡ 1 modulo all small irreducibles
connection: Over F_q[T], the analogue of lcm(1..k)+1 is P = ∏_{deg ≤ d} (irreducibles) + 1 (or ≡ 1 mod their product); the campaign's F_q[T] ES variants (FUNCTIONFIELD_ES*.md) could be fingerprinted on such P.
why: If F_q[T] ES counts at these P are minimal, the 'p ≡ 1 mod smooth' hardness mechanism is structural and transfers to the setting where proofs exist — a template for transferring arguments.
first_step: Using the existing F_q[T] engines (scripts/*ff*), count solutions at P = 1 + T·∏… for q = 3, 5 and compare with random P of the same degree.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Function-field analogue of the χ_p Euler-product law
connection: Over F_q[T], fit the ES count at monic irreducible P against Σ_{deg Q ≤ d} χ_P(Q)/|Q| (quadratic character of small-degree irreducibles mod P).
why: If the same law (negative α for 'P ≡ 1 mod 4'-analogue) holds, the count mechanism (Brauer/Hilbert symbol) is characteristic-free and the function-field proofs might reveal how to beat it.
first_step: Pick q = 3, deg P ≤ 10 (≈ 6 000 irreducibles); reuse the F_q[T] solution counters.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Pseudosquares over F_q[T] (Lehmer analogue) as the hardest ES inputs
connection: Define F_q[T] pseudosquares (non-square P ≡ square-like mod all small irreducibles); predicted hardest ES inputs if the integer picture transfers.
why: Bridges the integer pseudosquare fingerprint to the setting with proved ES variants.
first_step: Generate F_3[T] pseudosquares up to degree 12 and run the ES solvers.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Splitting fields of auxiliary polynomials
connection: For polynomial subfamilies of auxiliary values, relate factor-residue behavior to splitting in explicitly computed number fields.
why: Field structure may organize observed factor patterns, though integer prime divisors need separate analysis.
first_step: Compute a splitting field for one quadratic auxiliary polynomial and state precisely which finite-field splitting event is relevant.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Transfer matrices for bounded factor states
connection: Count admissible divisor selections with a transfer matrix whose state records residue and used multiplicities.
why: This exactly computes bounded subset-product counts and exposes repeated local blocks.
first_step: Build a transfer matrix for each prime-power factor and multiply them for one auxiliary integer.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Refactorization and Yang–Baxter leads
connection: Search for different factorizations of the same elementary matrix product that exchange parameter triples.
why: Refactorization produces exact rational transformations whose congruence effects can be examined.
first_step: Solve a three-factor matrix equality in two different orders and check whether the resulting map has an ES-admissible domain.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Cox-ring-inspired monomial bookkeeping
connection: Ask whether divisor classes on a simple compactification suggest a useful multigrading of parameter monomials.
why: A multigrading can explain which substitutions preserve the equation and boundary conditions.
first_step: For a basic rational surface chart, assign formal divisor degrees to denominator factors and check homogeneity of the cleared relation.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Sum–product over residue rings
connection: Explore additive and multiplicative expansion in Z/mZ while stratifying by ideals and zero divisors.
why: Composite moduli are intrinsic to many certificate conditions, so field-only models may omit essential structure.
first_step: For m=12,20,24, compute sumsets and product sets of actual attainable residue sets within each gcd stratum.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Dual certificates for relaxed parameter cones
connection: Use linear-programming duality to explain infeasibility of a specific linear relaxation of an auxiliary family.
why: A short dual identity can suggest which constraint must change, while remaining strictly local to that ansatz.
first_step: For one small infeasible linearized instance, compute a rational Farkas certificate and interpret each multiplier arithmetically.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Anderson localization analogy: ES certificate as an extended state
connection: The residue-class constraint f ≡ −p (mod 4cd) with f | p²+4c²d resembles a disordered 1-D hopping problem (random 'potential' from the factorization of p²+4c²d); a solution is a resonant state.
why: Localization theory proves existence of extended/localized states for *all* realizations via Furstenberg/Kotani (deterministic, not average), which is pointwise-in-disorder technology.
first_step: Define the transfer matrix M_c = product over prime factors of p²+4c²d of 2×2 matrices encoding the residue mod 4cd, and compute Lyapunov exponents; see if 'λ = 0 at some c' correlates with ES solutions.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Higher-order relaxations: (ℤ/4C)^× modulo k-th powers for k = 4, 8 — a tower of linear relaxations
connection: Beyond the F₂ (genus) relaxation, consider the quotient by 4th powers (ℤ/4-modules, with 'Rédei symbols'); the Type-II condition mod 4th powers is a ℤ/4-linear condition. The repo has bsB_redei_oddpart; the tower idea is to see at which level the relaxation becomes 'tight' with the true condition.
why: If the condition becomes tight at a bounded level (e.g. mod 8th powers), ES reduces to a ℤ/8-linear statement about Rédei-type symbols — rigid, computable, and maybe provable via reciprocity laws of higher degree.
first_step: Compute, for p ≤ 10⁴, C ≤ 50: level k at which the 'k-th power relaxation' condition agrees with the true win/fail; histogram.

title: Binary cubic forms: Delone–Faddeev and ES certificates as cubic rings

title: The numerator set M(p) is divisor-closed, so ES ⇔ M(p) contains a multiple of 4

connection: For each m, compute the n for which m/n is not a 3-term sum. Schinzel conjectures finiteness for each m. The growth of N(m) in m is the 'numerator direction' of the phase diagram.
why: If N(m) grows like exp(c√m) or polynomially, it constrains any uniform method (a method that works for m = 4 should work for all m with a predictable threshold).
first_step: Use the MO question's suggested n(k) viewpoint: compute largest failures for k=4,5,… over small ranges and test whether the same divisor-in-one-class parametrization extends uniformly in k.
alt_first_steps: [analogues-0121] Brute force m ≤ 30, n ≤ 10^5; record N(m) and exception counts; check literature for existing tables (e.g. Guy UPINT D11).
refs: Guy, Unsolved Problems in Number Theory, D11

title: Mordell–Schinzel for general m: are square classes obstructed for every numerator?
connection: For m = 4 square classes mod M admit no polynomial identities. Check whether the same holds for every m (and whether additional obstructed classes appear for composite m such as 8 or 12).
why: A uniform obstruction across m confirms that T1 is about squares, not about 4; extra obstructed classes for some m would be new phenomena.
first_step: Run the identity-coverage search for m = 5..12 modulo 840·k and list uncovered classes; compare with squares.

title: Numerator ladder 4 | 8 | 16 | …: ES(4·2^j) ⇒ ES(4) and exceptions grow with j
connection: By divisor-closure, 2^{j+2}/p solvable ⇒ 4/p solvable. The exceptional sets E_j for m = 2^{j+2} grow with j; ES ⇔ E_0 = ∅. Data at j = 1 (m = 8): {17, 241} below 4000.
why: Studying how E_j shrinks as j decreases gives a 'descent' picture; a proof that E_{j} ⊆ (explicit finite set) ∪ E_{j+1}... is not obviously helpful, but the E_j structure may reveal which primes are intrinsically hard.
first_step: Compute E_1, E_2 (m = 8, 16) for p < 10^5 and check whether hard ES primes (few solutions, e.g. 5, 13, 17, 193) are in all E_j.
refs: scripts/z52b_analogues_constraints.py (p ≡ 1 mod 4, p < 4000, all solutions enumerated)

title: Best underapproximation of 4/n by three unit fractions (Kovač / Nathanson / Chu) — ES ⇔ gap 0
connection: The 'best k-term underapproximation' literature studies max{Σ_{i≤k} 1/x_i ≤ q}. ES ⇔ the 3-term underapproximation of 4/n is exact. Structure theorems for best underapproximations (eventually greedy) might constrain when exactness is possible.
why: If best 3-term underapproximations of 4/n are 'eventually greedy' in a way that forces a particular x, ES reduces to a single e-slice — testable.
first_step: Read Kovač 2406.07218 and Nathanson 2202.00191; compute the best 3-term underapproximation of 4/p for p ≤ 10^4 and check whether greedy first term works.

title: Odd greedy algorithm (open termination problem) ↔ odd-denominator Egyptian fractions
connection: Every rational with odd denominator is a finite sum of distinct odd unit fractions (Breusch / Stewart, to check), but whether the odd greedy algorithm terminates is a famous open problem. ES with odd denominators is impossible (2-adic), but 4/n with an even number of odd terms (two can suffice, e.g. 4/15 = 1/5 + 1/15) is a natural neighbour.
why: Two open problems about restricted Egyptian expansions; techniques from one (e.g. 2-adic descent) may cross over.
first_step: Check the status of the odd greedy problem and of 'minimal number of odd unit fractions for 4/n' (must be even by parity); compute for n ≤ 1000.

title: Odd unit fractions for 4/n: parity forces an EVEN number of terms (2 is sometimes enough)
connection: A sum of k odd unit fractions has numerator Σ_i Π_{j≠i} x_j ≡ k (mod 2) over an odd denominator; since 4/n (n odd) has even numerator, k must be even. k = 2 sometimes works (4/15 = 1/5 + 1/15); otherwise k = 4 is the next option.
why: A 4-term odd-denominator ES ('4/n = four odd unit fractions') is a natural open-looking twin; determine whether it is always solvable when the 2-term version fails.
first_step: Compute for odd n ≤ 10^4 whether 4/n is a sum of two, else four, odd unit fractions; look for obstructions mod 8.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Shifted-prime denominators (Bloom): 4/n with denominators of the form q − 1, q prime
connection: Bloom proved results on unit fractions with shifted prime denominators (density/Ramsey type). The 3-term restriction 4/n = Σ 1/(q_i − 1) is a sparse constrained world.
why: A sparse world where heuristics predict finitely many solutions overall tests the lottery model calibration (expected count ≪ 1 gives failures).
first_step: Compute the expected number of solutions under the lottery model and compare with brute force for n ≤ 10^4.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Covering systems ↔ unit fractions (Z.-W. Sun): ES as a statement about AP packings
connection: Sun relates m-covers by residue classes to sums of unit fractions of moduli. Three pairwise disjoint APs with moduli x, y, z have density Σ 1/x_i; ES ⇔ some disjoint triple of APs has density exactly 4/n (disjointness needs at least pairwise gcd > 1, but this is neither automatic — (2,5,10) is an ES triple at n = 5 with gcd(2,5) = 1 — nor sufficient: periods (6,10,14) admit no three pairwise disjoint APs, since that would need three distinct parities).
why: Imports covering-system technology (Hough, Balister–Bollobás–Morris–Sahasrabudhe–Tiba distortion method) into ES via packings.
first_step: Determine for which ES triples disjoint residues exist (a CRT/graph-colouring condition on the gcds) and whether every p has at least one such triple; only then is 'ES ⇔ AP packing' an equivalence.

title: Four-term ES with distinct denominators is trivial — but four-term with a size cap is not
connection: 4/n as a sum of 4 unit fractions is easy (e.g. via 3/n splitting). With all denominators ≤ C·n (no huge denominators), the 4-term problem becomes a lattice/lottery problem again.
why: Size-capped multi-term ES might be provable for k = 4 with C large while ES (k = 3) remains open, giving a tunable intermediate theorem.
first_step: Compute, for n ≤ 10^4, the least C such that 4/n has a 4-term representation with max denominator ≤ C n; test boundedness.

title: A₃(p)-numerator geometry: the set M(p) as lattice points under a hyperbola
connection: m ∈ M(p) iff m/p = Σ 1/x_i; for each Type II parameter set, the achievable m form arithmetic progressions. M(p) is then a union of APs intersected with [1, 3p].
why: If M(p) is a union of many APs with differences coprime to 4, it contains a multiple of 4 — a pigeonhole route to ES via the numerator direction.
first_step: For p ≤ 10^4 compute M(p) and fit it as a union of APs; inspect the differences mod 4.

title: Rational numbers representable with three unit fractions: density among a/b with b ≤ N
connection: Most rationals a/b with a large are not 3-term sums. ES says all 4/n are. Placing 4/n in the 2D picture (a, b) shows ES is on a 'ray' where the density is 1 conjecturally.
why: If density along the ray a = 4 is provably 1 (Vaughan) and along a = c log b provably 0, the transition curve is a precise target for heuristics.
first_step: Compute, for b ≤ 2000, the proportion of representable a/b as a function of a; plot transition.

title: Greedy / Engel / Sylvester expansions as dynamical systems on rationals
connection: The greedy (Fibonacci–Sylvester) algorithm and Engel/Pierce expansions are dynamical maps on ℚ ∩ (0,1). ES asks for a 3-step orbit-like decomposition, not necessarily greedy.
why: Odd greedy and other algorithms have termination theorems and counterexample families. An algorithm with provable 3-step termination on 4/p would prove ES.
first_step: Test 'greedy with a bounded look-ahead' algorithms (choose x among the first K candidates ≥ ⌈p/4⌉) for 3-term termination at all p < 10⁸; find the minimal K(p) growth.
alt_first_steps: [analogues-0148] Implement 'greedy with first term chosen from {⌈n/4⌉ + j : j ≤ J}' and find the least J(p) for which the remainder is a 2-term sum; study J(p) growth.
[dividing-0150] Characterise the p for which some 'greedy with one free choice' algorithm gives 3 terms; compare with Mordell's classes.
[free_astra-0289] Derive the first two greedy residual numerators in each p modulo 4 case and factor their denominators.
[free_opus-0006] Compute for primes p ≡ 1 (mod 24) ≤ 10⁷ the fraction where greedy-with-one-alternative-first-step gives 3 terms; fit vs log p.

title: ES for numerators m that are prime vs composite (4 composite, 5 prime)
connection: Divisor-closure links composite numerators to their divisors; a prime numerator m has no proper non-trivial divisor (except 1). Compare exception structures across prime and composite m.
why: If composite m are systematically 'easier' through factor structure, the integer statement 'ES(4) ⇐ ES(2)-type subproblems' may have a useful partial version.
first_step: Using the Schinzel table item, compare exception counts for m prime vs composite at fixed n-range.

title: Kraft–McMillan / compact trees ↔ sums of unit fractions (Elsholtz–Heuberger–Prodinger)
connection: Compact prefix codes and canonical trees are counted via sums of unit fractions; ES-type identities appear as specific tree shapes with three leaves of weights 1/x_i summing to 4/n.
why: A tree/code interpretation may give a bijective or generating-function handle on solution counts.
first_step: Read arXiv:1108.5964 to see which unit-fraction equations correspond to which trees; check whether 3-leaf subtrees encode ES.

title: Egyptian fractions in the Sierpiński triangle / Pascal mod 2
connection: Recent work connects Egyptian fractions to the Sierpiński triangle (De Carli et al.). A 2-adic/Lucas-theorem structure might organize 4/n representations by binary digits of n.
why: The 2-adic structure of ES (coordinate in 4Z ∪ (8Z − p), m = 8 coincidence) could match Pascal-mod-2 patterns.
first_step: Read arXiv:2412.09728 to see the precise correspondence and test whether ES solution counts correlate with binary digit patterns of p.

title: Numerator-8 and 4 | denominator coincidence: test an explicit bijection between the two solution sets
connection: Up to 2·10^4 both 'all denominators even' (⇔ 8/p) and 'some denominator ≡ 0 mod 4' fail exactly at {17, 241}. A map: a solution of 8/p (x', y', z') gives 4/p with (2x', 2y', 2z'); does every solution with 4 | x arise from some all-even solution and vice versa?
why: An exact bijection would be a 2-adic structural theorem about ES; if not exact, the coincidence of failure sets is still a strong hint of a local mechanism.
first_step: For p < 2000, compute both solution sets and test whether 'has a solution with 4 | some denominator' ⇔ 'has an all-even solution' solution-by-solution (not just existence).

title: Prime-power numerators: m = 4 = 2² vs m = 9, 25, 49 — do odd prime squares behave like 4?
connection: Divisor-closure: 9/p solvable ⇒ 3/p solvable (trivial). For m = ℓ², the 'hard part' is ℓ² itself. Compare exception sets for m = 9, 25 with ES.
why: If m = ℓ² is generally easy except for ℓ = 2, then the dyadic nature of 4 matters; if m = 9 has square-class obstructions too, T1 is uniform.
first_step: Compute exceptions of 9/n and 25/n (3 terms) for n ≤ 10^5; compare with Mordell-type identity coverage modulo 840·k.

title: Croot's colouring theorem and Bloom's density theorem: Egyptian existence in dense sets
connection: Croot proved that any finite colouring of ℕ has a monochromatic set with reciprocal sum 1; Bloom proved that sets of positive upper density contain such sets. The method (Fourier analysis on smooth numbers, many terms) fails for 3 terms.
why: Their 'smooth-number Fourier' technology might yield 'k-term ES with denominators in a dense set' for bounded but large k, a new intermediate theorem.
first_step: Check Liu–Sawhney 'further questions' for bounded-length results with dense denominators.
alt_first_steps: [signature-0046] Identify the step in Bloom where many terms are needed and ask if a 3-term version with target 4/p survives under a smooth-number restriction.
refs: unverified: Croot 2003, On a coloring conjecture about unit fractions (Annals 157)

title: Conlon–Fox–He on an Erdős–Graham question about Egyptian fractions
connection: Recent work resolves an Erdős–Graham question on Egyptian fractions (details to read). It belongs to the modern 'Egyptian existence' toolkit along with Bloom and Liu–Sawhney.
why: Any new technique giving existence of Egyptian representations with structural constraints is a candidate input for constrained ES worlds.
first_step: Read arXiv:2404.16016 abstract and main theorem; note the technique.

title: Odd perfect numbers and abundancy: Σ_{d | n} 1/d = 2 as an Egyptian constraint
connection: σ(n)/n = Σ_{d|n} 1/d; perfect numbers solve an Egyptian equation with denominators forced to be all divisors. Bounds on odd perfect numbers (Nielsen) use unit-fraction inequalities.
why: Shares the 'Egyptian equation + multiplicative constraint' shape; techniques bounding solutions there bound ES-like constrained worlds.
first_step: Low priority: note as sibling.

title: Erdős–Selfridge/Graham 'Egyptian fractions with denominators in [N, cN]' as size-window sibling
connection: Problems asking for Σ 1/x_i = 1 with all x_i in a dyadic range relate to ES solutions whose denominators are confined to windows (p/4 < x ≤ 3p/4 etc.).
why: Window-confined existence results (Croot) are the closest analytic sibling to the ES window/slice structure.
first_step: Pointer: compare with Croot's short-interval result (batch C).

title: Sierpiński's 5/n, Schinzel's m/n: almost-all results (Vaughan) are uniform in m — what uniformity is known?
connection: Vaughan's density result covers every fixed m. The dependence of the exceptional-set bound on m is the quantitative sibling link between ES and its numerator neighbours.
why: A bound uniform in m up to (log n)^A would show the numerator-ladder (4 | 8 | 16) exceptional sets shrink together.
first_step: Read Vaughan 1970 for m-dependence; record.

title: Counting Egyptian fractions (Bettin–Grenié–Molteni): number of k-term representations of 1
connection: Precise asymptotics/lower bounds for the number of k-term Egyptian representations exist; ES counts (Elsholtz–Tao) are the numerator-4 three-term analogue.
why: Their methods (lattice point counting with Dirichlet series) may give secondary terms for ES average counts, sharpening the lottery mean.
first_step: Read arXiv:1906.11986 / 2509.10030 for methods; compare with Elsholtz–Tao's average counts.

title: All denominators divisible by 3 ⇔ 12/p is a 3-term sum: fails at 15 primes below 8000
connection: Analogous to all-even ⇔ 8/p: 'all denominators ≡ 0 mod 3' ⇔ 12/p = Σ 1/(x_i/3). Failures: 5, 13, 29, 37, 73, 97, 193, 433, 577, 1129, … (15 of 499).
why: The numerator ladder m ∈ {4, 8, 12, 16, …} gives nested strengthenings with growing (apparently finite?) exceptional sets; their structure across m (Schinzel) tells how robust ES is.
first_step: Extend to 10^5 and check whether the m = 12 exceptional set stabilizes (finite) or keeps growing; compare with m = 8 ({17, 241}).

title: Dyadic world Z[1/2] variant with 4 NOT a unit: replace numerator by 3 over Z[1/3]
connection: Over Z[1/3] the numerator 3 is a unit, mirroring Z[1/2] for 4. The hard analogue would be '3/n over ℕ' — but 3/n is trivial over ℕ. So the pair (numerator, inverted prime) = (4, 2) is special: 4 is a prime power of the smallest prime.
why: Highlights that ES's numerator is a power of the prime 2 that also controls the parity/2-adic structure; any 'ℓ-analogue' of ES is ℓ²/n with ℓ odd (see prime-squares item).
first_step: Context; tie to the m = 9, 25 computations.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Partial-fraction world: 4/(T(T+1)(T+2)…) in Q(T) — Egyptian decompositions of rational functions
connection: Partial fractions decompose rational functions into sums of simple fractions A/(T − a). An 'Egyptian' decomposition requires numerators 1 and denominators in a semiring (e.g. monic polynomials with positive roots). This is a characteristic-0 FF-like world with residues.
why: Residue calculus gives exact conditions: Σ residues = coefficient conditions; may reveal a residue obstruction analogous to Lemma 1.1.
first_step: Determine when 4/(T − a) = Σ 1/X_i(T) with X_i monic in R[T] having real positive roots; compute residue constraints.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Coding-theoretic world: ES as a weight-enumerator identity for three cyclic codes of lengths x, y, z
connection: A cyclic code of length x has 'density' 1/x for a single codeword position class; a disjoint union of three such position classes with total density 4/n is the AP packing reformulation in coding language.
why: Mostly a rephrasing of the AP packing world; little added value.
first_step: Low priority.

title: k = 4 positive terms with all denominators ≡ 0 mod 4? ⇔ 16/n as a 4-term sum
connection: Generalizing all-even ⇔ 8/p: 4-term representations with all denominators divisible by 4 ⇔ 16/n is a 4-term sum. Divisor-closure across k-term worlds: (4d)/n with k terms ⇒ 4/n with k terms.
why: A k-term numerator ladder with k = 4 might be provable (more freedom), providing 4-term ES for all n — and a 4 → 3 merging step would be needed.
first_step: Compute exceptions of 16/n as a 4-term sum for n ≤ 10^4.
